title: Bash Arrays & Parameters: The Dense-Notes Field Guide
summary: Ten dense pages taking you from shell-variable fundamentals through indexed and associative arrays, the $@/$* split, the full parameter-expansion toolkit, and local-variable scoping in functions, with worked idioms, comparisons, and the classic bugs.

chapters.title: Shell Variables: The Ground Floor
points: A Bash variable holds a string; types are bolted on with declare: -i integer, -a indexed array, -A associative array.
Assignment syntax: name=value with NO spaces around the =; name = value instead runs the command `name` with argument `=`.
Valid names: letters, digits, underscores, not starting with a digit; variables are case-sensitive.
Expand with $name or ${name}; braces are required when gluing text: ${file}bak, because $filebak looks up a variable named filebak.
An unset variable expands to the empty string — Bash has no null; set -u turns any unset expansion into a hard error.
Unquoted expansions get word-split on IFS then glob-expanded; "double quotes" keep one value as one word — quote every expansion by default.
export name=value copies the variable into child processes; a child that changes it changes only its own copy.
readonly NAME=... blocks later assignment; unset on a readonly variable fails.
var=$(command) captures stdout into the variable, stripping trailing newlines; the legacy backtick form does the same with worse nesting.
Plain assignment creates a global; declare and local create attributed or scoped variables.
Gotcha: var=value command sets var only in that command's environment — the current shell keeps its old value.
Arithmetic lives elsewhere: $((x+1)) or ((x++)); variables stay strings until math coerces them.

chapters.title: Indexed Arrays: Creation & Anatomy
points: An indexed array is an ordered map from integers to strings; valid subscripts start at 0.
Literal form: fruits=(apple banana cherry) — parentheses make the array, spaces separate elements.
The assignment alone creates the array; declare -a is optional and only adds clarity or attributes.
Explicit subscripts: arr=([2]=a [0]=b) — order inside the literal does not matter and indices need not be dense.
Element assignment: arr[3]=x; the subscript is an arithmetic context, so arr[i+1]=y just works.
Negative subscripts count from the end: arr[-1] is the last element, arr[-2] the one before (Bash 4.3+).
Append with arr+=(orange); merge whole arrays with arr+=("${other[@]}") — appending never renumbers existing elements.
Arrays are sparse: arr[1000]=x gives ${#arr[@]} equal to 1; holes cost nothing and are never auto-filled.
Quote elements containing spaces: crew=("Ada Lovelace" "Grace Hopper") keeps each person one element.
Reassignment replaces the whole array: arr=(a b) discards every previous element.
unset arr[1] deletes a single element and leaves a hole; unset arr deletes the entire variable.
Elements are always strings: nums=(42 3.14 hello) stores text — no numeric coercion at storage time.

chapters.title: Reading, Iterating & Slicing Arrays
points: Read one element as ${arr[i]} — braces are mandatory: $arr[i] expands $arr and then prints a literal [i].
"${arr[@]}" expands to each element as its own word; "${arr[*]}" expands to ONE word joined by the first character of IFS.
${#arr[@]} counts set elements (sparse-aware); ${#arr[i]} gives the length of one element.
The safe loop: for x in "${arr[@]}"; do ... — the quoting is exactly what keeps "Ada Lovelace" a single item.
Index loop: for i in "${!arr[@]}"; do echo "$i: ${arr[$i]}"; done — the robust walk over sparse arrays.
"${!arr[@]}" lists existing subscripts in ascending numeric order — perfect for holes like arr=([1]=a [5]=b).
Last element: "${arr[-1]}" (4.3+) or "${arr[@]: -1}" — the space matters, because "${arr[@]:-1}" parses as the default operator.
Slices: "${arr[@]:2:3}" is three elements starting at index 2; "${arr[@]: -2}" is the final two.
C-style loop for ((i=0; i<${#arr[@]}; i++)) assumes dense 0..n-1 indices — it misfires on sparse arrays.
File to array: mapfile -t lines < file.txt (Bash 4+) splits on newlines, strips them, keeps empty lines.
Portable alternative: while IFS= read -r line; do lines+=("$line"); done < file.txt.
Classic bug: for x in ${arr[@]} unquoted re-splits every element on whitespace and expands any glob characters inside.
Empty arrays vs set -u: "${arr[@]}" errors on Bash older than 4.4; guard with ${arr[@]+"${arr[@]}"}.

chapters.title: Associative Arrays: Key-Value Maps
points: An associative array maps arbitrary string keys to values; Bash requires declare -A caps before the first assignment.
Assign pair by pair: caps[db]=postgres; or in one literal: caps=( [db]=postgres [web]=nginx ).
Quote keys with spaces or punctuation: ages["Ada Lovelace"]=36 — the key is taken literally, no glob expansion.
Read with ${caps[db]}; the whole expansion wears braces, the key wears square brackets.
${#caps[@]} counts pairs; "${!caps[@]}" lists keys in hash order — never insertion order, so sort for stable output.
Existence check: [[ -v caps[db] ]] or ${caps[db]+x} — distinguishes a missing key from one holding an empty string.
Pair iteration: for k in "${!caps[@]}"; do echo "$k = ${caps[$k]}"; done.
unset caps[db] removes one pair; unset caps removes the whole map.
Counter idiom: count[$w]=$(( ${count[$w]:-0} + 1 )) — the :-0 default is what makes first-seen keys work.
Use as lookup tables to replace long case/if chains: option flags, host-to-ip maps, grouping records by field.
Trap: without declare -A, x[key]=v builds an INDEXED array — key is evaluated as arithmetic, landing on index 0 unless key names a numeric variable.
Trade-off: indexed arrays keep order and slice cleanly; associative arrays give named constant-time lookup but no ordering and no slicing.

chapters.title: Positional Parameters & the $@ vs $* Split
points: Positional parameters $1..$9 are direct; from the tenth on you need braces: ${10} — plain $10 parses as ${1} glued to a literal 0.
$0 is the script name, $# is the argument count, shift n discards the first n arguments and renumbers the rest.
$@ and $* both mean all positionals; they behave differently ONLY inside double quotes.
"$@": each parameter becomes a separate word, individually quoted — an argument "hello world" stays one word.
"$*": all parameters become ONE word, joined by the first character of IFS (a space by default).
Unquoted $@ and $* are identical — both get word-split and globbed; the classic bug is missing quotes, not the wrong symbol.
With zero arguments "$@" yields zero words while "$*" yields one empty word — visible in loops and [ ] tests.
Custom join: IFS=, ; echo "$*" prints a,b,c — great for messages, wrong for forwarding arguments onward.
The pass-through idiom: wrapper() { realcmd "$@"; } forwards arguments untouched — always quote.
Worked example, args = ("hello world" b): "$@" gives 2 words; "$*" gives "hello world b" as 1 word; unquoted $* re-splits into 3+ words.
Manual parsing loop: while (($#)); do case $1 in -v) verbose=1;; *) files+=("$1");; esac; shift; done.
Inside a function, $@, $# and shift operate on the function's own arguments — the script's are shadowed, not destroyed.

chapters.title: Parameter Expansion I: Defaults & Alternates
points: Parameter expansion is the ${name...} operator family: evaluated at expansion time, inside the shell, zero subprocesses.
${var:-word}: expands to word when var is unset OR empty; otherwise to var — the everyday default guard.
${var-word}: substitutes only when var is UNSET; a set-but-empty var stays empty — the colon means "also treat empty as unset".
${var:=word}: same test as :- but ALSO assigns word back to var, so the default persists for later lines.
${var:+word}: the inverse — expands to word only when var is set AND non-empty; otherwise nothing.
${var:?msg}: on unset/empty prints msg to stderr and aborts the script — assert required input early: : "${1:?need a file}".
Memory hook: no colon = unset only; colon = unset or empty; the trailing symbol picks the action (- use, = assign, + replace, ? die).
Defaults evaluate lazily and nest: ${PORT:-$(awk '/port/{print $2}' cfg)} runs the command only when PORT is missing.
Defaults work on positionals: outfile=${1:-output.txt} sets a fallback first argument in one line.
:- never mutates the variable; := does — picking the wrong one causes state surprises.
Quote guarded defaults with spaces: dir="${1:-./my folder}" keeps the fallback a single word.
Chain fallbacks: ${A:-${B:-fallback}} resolves to the first non-empty of A, B, fallback.

chapters.title: Parameter Expansion II: Trim, Replace, Case
points: Front trims: ${var#pat} deletes the SHORTEST leading match; ${var##pat} deletes the LONGEST (greedy).
End trims: ${var%pat} shortest trailing match; ${var%%pat} longest trailing match.
Mnemonic: # comments at the front, so it trims the front; % sits at the end, so it trims the end; doubled sign = longest match.
Patterns are globs, not regex: *, ?, [abc], [0-9]; there are no capture groups or alternation.
basename in one expansion: file=${path##*/}; dirname: dir=${path%/*}.
Extensions: name=${file%.*} strips the last one; ext=${file##*.} keeps it — archive.tar.gz becomes archive.tar plus gz.
No match, no change: every trim returns the original value untouched when the pattern fails — safe to apply unconditionally.
Replacement: ${var/old/new} swaps the first occurrence; ${var//old/new} swaps all of them.
Anchored replacement: ${var/#old/new} pins to the start, ${var/%old/new} pins to the end.
Delete by substituting the empty string: ${var//-/} removes dashes; ${var// /_} turns spaces into underscores.
Bash 4 case ops: ${var^^} all upper, ${var,,} all lower, ${var^} uppercases the first character, ${var,} lowercases it.
Versus external tools: sed/awk/tr/cut each fork a process; expansions run in-process — in loops the difference is milliseconds vs microseconds.

chapters.title: Substrings, Indirection & the Cost Model
points: Substring: ${var:offset:length}, zero-based; omit length to run to the end: ${var:0:3}.
Negative offsets count from the end but need a space or parens: ${var: -4} or ${var:(-4)} — ${var:-4} means 'default 4'.
Negative length (Bash 4.2+): ${var:2:-3} stops three characters before the end.
The same operator slices arrays by elements: "${arr[@]:1:2}" is two elements starting at index 1.
Indirection: ${!name} uses the VALUE of name as a variable NAME — n=color; ${!n} yields the value of color.
Indirection replaces most eval uses — no double parsing, no injection surface.
Name listing: "${!prefix@}" expands to every variable name starting with prefix — handy for grouped config vars.
Offsets and subscripts are arithmetic contexts: ${arr[i+1]}, ${var:i*2:4} — no extra $(( )) wrapping needed.
Operators do not nest: ${${v#a}/x/y} is a syntax error — assign an intermediate: t=${v#a}; then ${t/x/y}.
Cost model: expansions are in-process and take microseconds; each sed/cut/subshell forks a process — inside loops, prefer built-ins.

chapters.title: Functions, local & Variable Scope
points: Define with POSIX syntax: greet() { echo "hi, $1"; } — call it like a command: greet world.
Without local, every assignment inside a function overwrites the global variable of that name.
local x (or local x=0) scopes the name to the function; it disappears when the function returns.
Bash uses dynamic scoping: a callee sees the caller's locals — inner functions can read the outer function's private names.
local is a command and masks exit statuses: local v=$(cmd) always succeeds — split declare and assignment to test cmd.
return N is a 0-255 STATUS, not data; send data out via stdout, or by writing to a caller's variable.
Consuming stdout with var=$(func) runs the function in a subshell — its local and global writes are lost.
Pass arrays in as arguments: sum "${nums[@]}"; rebuild inside with local -a a=("$@").
Get arrays out via nameref (Bash 4.3+): fill() { local -n ref=$1; ref=(a b c); }; call fill myarr.
Recursion works because locals give each frame its own variables; there is no tail-call optimization, so depth is finite.
Pipe trap: cmd | while read -r x; ... runs the loop in a subshell — counters set inside vanish; use done < <(cmd) instead.
Attributes combine with local: local -i n=0 integer, local -a arr indexed, local -A map associative.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & the Field Recap
points: Scalar slip: arr="one two" makes a string; arr=(one two) makes an array — the parentheses are the whole difference.
Most common bug in the wild: unquoted "$@" or "${arr[@]}" — word splitting plus globbing quietly mangles values with spaces or *.
$arr[i] expands $arr first and prints value[i]; element access always needs the braces: ${arr[i]}.
"$*" in a forwarding call silently merges arguments — reserve it for display, use "$@" to pass along.
dict[key]=value without declare -A silently builds an indexed array (the key evaluates as arithmetic and lands on 0).
:- vs -: decide whether an EMPTY value counts as missing; get it wrong and legitimate empty inputs get defaulted.
${var: -4} needs the space — ${var:-4} is parsed as 'use 4 if unset'.
Order assumptions: "${!caps[@]}" is hash order, not insertion order — sort it or keep a parallel indexed array of keys.
arr=() empties the array but keeps its type; unset arr destroys the variable and its -A attribute — know which reset you mean.
Never for x in $(cat file) — it splits on every whitespace run; use mapfile or while read.
Subshell traps: pipes into while and $(...) discard variable updates — keep state in the main shell with process substitution.
Recap checklist: quote every expansion, declare -A before use, prefer ${ } over sed/awk in loops, local in every function, develop with set -u and shellcheck.
